entries.one_line: Hear, find, and use the notes of a key by the role they play—not just by their names.
entries.overview: Every note in a key has a relationship to its tonal center, the note that feels like home. Scale-degree recognition means noticing that relationship: by ear, on the fretboard, in a melody, or while making musical choices. The number describes the note’s place relative to the tonic, so the idea travels with you when the key changes.
entries.key_distinction: A scale degree is measured relative to the tonic; chord membership is measured relative to the current chord. These are not the same label.

intro.text: Every note has a relationship to the
— the home note of a key. Scale-degree recognition helps you hear, locate, and choose those relationships on purpose.

learning_levels.title: Foundational
learning_levels.goal: Establish a tonal center, number the notes of a key, and recognize a few stable reference points.

learning_levels.title: Intermediate
learning_levels.goal: Recognize less obvious degrees, change keys, and apply the relationships in melodies.

learning_levels.title: Advanced
learning_levels.goal: Track tonal relationships through changing harmony and use them intentionally in musical decisions.

applications.title: Aural recognition
applications.summary: Hear where a note sits relative to a tonal center.

applications.title: Fretboard navigation
applications.summary: Locate scale degrees without relying on one memorized shape.

applications.title: Theory & function
applications.summary: Describe tonal roles and distinguish scale degrees from chord tones.

applications.title: Improvisation
applications.summary: Choose notes for arrival, motion, and tension in real time.

applications.title: Composition
applications.summary: Shape melodic expectations with scale-degree choices.

modules.title: Hear the tonal home
outcomes: Keep C in mind as a tonic
Compare 1, 3, and 5 against that tonic
modules.explanation: Start with C as home. In C major, C is 1, E is 3, and G is 5. Over a sustained C, these are useful reference points. Their character changes when the harmony or key changes.

exercises.title: Find home
exercises.setup: Use a quiet C drone or repeatedly play C on your guitar.
steps: Play or sing C and call it 1.
Play E and G, naming 3 and 5.
Close your eyes, play one of the three, and name its scale degree.
Confirm by replaying C, then your target.
exercises.self_check: Can you identify the relationship to C without guessing from finger position?

steps: Play or sing C and call it 1.
Play E and G, naming 3 and 5.
Close your eyes, play one of the three, and name its scale degree.
Confirm by replaying C, then your target.

modules.title: Number a major scale
outcomes: Label all seven degrees in one major key
Separate note name from relative degree
modules.explanation: In C major the notes C D E F G A B correspond to 1 2 3 4 5 6 7. In G major, G is 1 and B is 3. A degree number stays meaningful when the notes change with the key.

exercises.title: Number the scale
exercises.setup: Write a one-octave C-major scale on paper or in a Workbook.
steps: Label C as 1 and continue to B as 7.
Switch to G major and label G through F♯.
Cover the numbers and reconstruct them.
exercises.self_check: Can you find degree 3 in both keys without using the same letter name?

steps: Label C as 1 and continue to B as 7.
Switch to G major and label G through F♯.
Cover the numbers and reconstruct them.

modules.title: Locate 1, 3, and 5
outcomes: Find the tonic in more than one place
Locate major scale degrees 3 and 5 relative to it
modules.explanation: In C major, the tonic C is your reference; E and G are degrees 3 and 5. Try one string set, then locate the same relationships elsewhere on the neck.

exercises.title: Three notes, multiple locations
exercises.setup: Use standard tuning and C major; no speed target.
steps: Find C, E, and G on the first two strings.
Find another C elsewhere on the instrument.
Without reading note names, identify which played note is 1, 3, or 5.
exercises.self_check: Can you name the degree and the pitch separately?

steps: Find C, E, and G on the first two strings.
Find another C elsewhere on the instrument.
Without reading note names, identify which played note is 1, 3, or 5.

modules.title: Hear the other degrees
outcomes: Compare 2, 4, 6, and 7 with tonic
Identify short patterns with a tonal center
modules.explanation: Try D, F, A, and B against C as home. Notice their different colors and likely melodic movements. These tendencies depend on the musical context; they are not fixed emotional rules.

exercises.title: The four colors
exercises.setup: Keep a C tonic sounding clearly.
steps: Alternate C→D→C, C→F→E, C→A→G, and C→B→C.
Sing the target degree before playing it.
Change the order, then identify each by its relationship to C.
exercises.self_check: Does recognizing the degree survive when you start on a different octave?

steps: Alternate C→D→C, C→F→E, C→A→G, and C→B→C.
Sing the target degree before playing it.
Change the order, then identify each by its relationship to C.

modules.title: Move the relationship to a new key
outcomes: Find the same degrees in two keys
Identify them across at least two positions
modules.explanation: The relationship—not a fret number—is the goal. Degree 3 in C major is E; degree 3 in G major is B. Move the tonal center and rebuild the degree map.

exercises.title: Keep the number, change the note
exercises.setup: Work in C major and G major in standard tuning.
steps: Locate 1, 3, 5, and 7 in C major on a chosen string pair.
Move to G major and locate 1, 3, 5, and 7 there.
Name the changing pitches and unchanged degrees.
exercises.self_check: Can you find degree 7 without tracing the entire scale shape?

steps: Locate 1, 3, 5, and 7 in C major on a chosen string pair.
Move to G major and locate 1, 3, 5, and 7 there.
Name the changing pitches and unchanged degrees.

modules.title: Separate scale degrees from chord tones
outcomes: Identify degree relative to the key
Identify whether it belongs to the current triad
modules.explanation: Scale-degree 3 in C major is always E while C remains the tonal center. But if the harmony moves to F major, E is not one of the F–A–C triad notes. Scale degree and chord-tone role are related but not identical.

exercises.title: One note, two relationships
exercises.setup: Use the progression C–F–G–C in C major.
steps: Choose E and identify it as scale degree 3 throughout.
Over each chord, decide whether E belongs to the chord triad.
Listen to E against C major and then F major.
exercises.self_check: Can you keep the key reference while hearing the local chord change?

steps: Choose E and identify it as scale degree 3 throughout.
Over each chord, decide whether E belongs to the chord triad.
Listen to E against C major and then F major.

modules.title: Aim a phrase at a degree
outcomes: Land deliberately on 1, 3, or 5
Describe the resulting melodic shape without claiming universal emotions
modules.explanation: Choose a destination note first, then build a short melodic path to it. Over C major, try landing on E (degree 3) or G (degree 5) and hear the difference from landing on C.

exercises.title: Three destinations
exercises.setup: Use a C-major vamp and a comfortable tempo.
steps: Improvise a two-bar phrase that ends on 1.
Repeat with an ending on 3, then on 5.
Record a note about which ending sounds finished or open to you.
exercises.self_check: Can you choose the destination before your fingers arrive?

steps: Improvise a two-bar phrase that ends on 1.
Repeat with an ending on 3, then on 5.
Record a note about which ending sounds finished or open to you.

modules.title: Track degrees through a moving progression
outcomes: Maintain a tonal reference across chord changes
Transcribe a short melodic outline in degrees
modules.explanation: A melody does not stop having scale degrees when the chords change underneath it. Follow the tonal center while also noticing how each note changes color against the local chord.

exercises.title: Degree-outline transcription
exercises.setup: Use an uncomplicated melody in C major over C–Am–F–G.
steps: Listen once and hum the melody.
Mark likely degrees for each melody note.
Check your outline on the guitar and revise what you heard.
Identify where the same scale degree changes harmonic role.
exercises.self_check: Can you explain the difference between degree-from-key and note-against-chord?

steps: Listen once and hum the melody.
Mark likely degrees for each melody note.
Check your outline on the guitar and revise what you heard.
Identify where the same scale degree changes harmonic role.

modules.title: Connect chord tones with intention
outcomes: Track degrees while harmony changes
Use approach notes that resolve into targets
modules.explanation: Plan your destination by both scale degree and chord membership. A single note can be familiar relative to the key and surprising relative to the current chord.

exercises.title: Target-note bridge
exercises.setup: Play over C–Am–F–G in C major.
steps: Mark a chord tone to target on each change.
Connect the targets with small stepwise movements.
Name the scale degrees of your targets.
Record which notes feel like anticipation or arrival in context.
exercises.self_check: Can you explain what the note does relative to the key and to the chord?

steps: Mark a chord tone to target on each change.
Connect the targets with small stepwise movements.
Name the scale degrees of your targets.
Record which notes feel like anticipation or arrival in context.

modules.title: Design melodic tension and release
outcomes: Compose one contrasting phrase pair
Explain a note choice as scale degree and musical context
modules.explanation: Write a short melody that deliberately postpones and then provides resolution. Treat these as compositional choices rather than fixed emotional labels for particular numbers.

exercises.title: Question and answer
exercises.setup: Choose C major and a slow, comfortable tempo.
steps: Write a two-bar phrase that ends somewhere other than 1.
Write a second phrase that responds and settles on 1.
Try the same melodic contour in another key.
Use a Workbook page to notate or tab the two phrases.
exercises.self_check: Can you describe what changed, and why you chose the final degree?

steps: Write a two-bar phrase that ends somewhere other than 1.
Write a second phrase that responds and settles on 1.
Try the same melodic contour in another key.
Use a Workbook page to notate or tab the two phrases.

relationships.why: Understanding the collection of notes makes numbering degrees easier.
A reference tonic is necessary to interpret a degree; the concept can be taught within the lesson.
Hearing pitch distances helps, but need not precede all degree-recognition work.
Basic note location supports pitch-to-degree mapping.
Mapping patterns provides one of several ways to visualize degrees.
Degree recognition supports intentional melodic note choice.
Scale degrees describe relationships used to shape melodies.

entries.one_line: Build three-note chords from the notes that give them their identity.
entries.overview: A triad is made from three different chord tones: a root, a third and a fifth. Change the third and you can change the chord from major to minor. Learn to name the notes first, then find and arrange them across the fretboard. You can use the same idea in any key.
entries.key_distinction: A chord root is not necessarily the tonic of the key. A triad can also be voiced in different orders (inversions), and octave doubling does not add a new chord tone.

intro.text: contains a root, a third, and a fifth. Changing the third changes a major chord to a minor chord while the root and perfect fifth remain.

learning_levels.title: Foundational
learning_levels.goal: Identify root, third and fifth; build major and minor triads; verify simple guitar voicings by note name.

learning_levels.title: Intermediate
learning_levels.goal: Reorder chord tones into inversions and recognize what major/minor quality sounds like.

learning_levels.title: Advanced
learning_levels.goal: Use minimal voice movement and deliberate voicing choices in a progression and original arrangement.

applications.title: Harmony & construction
applications.summary: Spell the three chord tones and understand chord quality.

applications.title: Fretboard shapes & inversions
applications.summary: Locate triads across string sets, inversions and tunings.

applications.title: Listening & chord quality
applications.summary: Hear what changes when the third moves between major and minor.

applications.title: Arrangement & voice leading
applications.summary: Use triads as connected melodic and harmonic voices.

modules.title: Find the three chord tones
outcomes: Spell C major and C minor correctly
Understand the effect of changing the third
modules.explanation: A major triad uses a root, a major third and a perfect fifth. A minor triad uses the same root and perfect fifth but replaces the major third with a minor third. For C, compare C–E–G with C–E♭–G.

exercises.title: Spell and compare
exercises.setup: Use note names; you do not need the instrument initially.
steps: Write C, E and G, and label root, third, fifth.
Move E down one semitone to E♭ without changing C or G.
Repeat with G major (G–B–D) and G minor (G–B♭–D).
Explain which interval changed and why.
exercises.self_check: Can you identify the only chord tone that changes between these major and minor pairs?

steps: Write C, E and G, and label root, third, fifth.
Move E down one semitone to E♭ without changing C or G.
Repeat with G major (G–B–D) and G minor (G–B♭–D).
Explain which interval changed and why.

modules.title: Find one major and minor triad on guitar
outcomes: Locate C major on strings 3–2–1
Change its quality without changing the root or fifth
modules.explanation: In standard tuning, fret 5 of the G string is C, fret 5 of the B string is E, and fret 3 of the high E string is G. Those three notes form C major. Lower the B-string note by one fret to E♭ for C minor.

exercises.title: The movable third
exercises.setup: Use standard tuning and only strings 3, 2 and 1.
steps: Play G-string fret 5, B-string fret 5, high-E fret 3: C–E–G.
Play the B string at fret 4 instead: C–E♭–G.
Name every note before you play it again.
Check the open-string tuning before trying another string set.
exercises.self_check: Can you explain the change without relying on the chord-shape silhouette?

steps: Play G-string fret 5, B-string fret 5, high-E fret 3: C–E–G.
Play the B string at fret 4 instead: C–E♭–G.
Name every note before you play it again.
Check the open-string tuning before trying another string set.

modules.title: Inversions: same notes, new bass
outcomes: Recognize root position and two inversions
Move among inversions while retaining chord identity
modules.explanation: A C major triad contains C, E and G in every inversion. C–E–G is root position; E–G–C and G–C–E are the first and second inversions. Guitar voicings can spread or double notes, so verify the actual pitches.

exercises.title: Reorder, then locate
exercises.setup: Write C–E–G on paper before moving to guitar.
steps: Write C–E–G, E–G–C and G–C–E; circle the lowest note each time.
Find each bass note on your chosen string set.
Find the other two chord tones nearby; write their string/fret positions.
Check each voicing against note names rather than a memorized shape.
exercises.self_check: Can you explain why these arrangements remain C major even when the bass note changes?

steps: Write C–E–G, E–G–C and G–C–E; circle the lowest note each time.
Find each bass note on your chosen string set.
Find the other two chord tones nearby; write their string/fret positions.
Check each voicing against note names rather than a memorized shape.

modules.title: Hear the difference between major and minor
outcomes: Distinguish a major third from a minor third
Compare major/minor quality against the same root
modules.explanation: The third is a major contributor to a triad’s quality. Keep C and G fixed while comparing E with E♭, and listen to the change without assigning a universal emotion to either chord.

exercises.title: One-note change
exercises.setup: Use a keyboard, carefully tuned guitar or notes played by a partner.
steps: Play or listen to C–E–G, then C–E♭–G with the same root and register.
Focus on which individual pitch changes between the two.
Cover the labels and alternate the two voicings in random order.
Reveal the labels only after naming the third.
exercises.self_check: Can you distinguish the changed third by ear when the register and dynamics stay similar?

steps: Play or listen to C–E–G, then C–E♭–G with the same root and register.
Focus on which individual pitch changes between the two.
Cover the labels and alternate the two voicings in random order.
Reveal the labels only after naming the third.

modules.title: Connect shapes with small voice movements
outcomes: Identify common tones across two chords
Choose voice movement based on note distance
modules.explanation: Voice leading means connecting individual chord tones from one harmony to the next. On the top three strings in standard tuning, C major at 5–5–3 can move to an F-major inversion at 5–6–5: C remains, E moves to F, and G moves to A. This is an example, not the only correct solution.

exercises.title: C major to F major
exercises.setup: Use standard tuning, strings 3–2–1 (G–B–E), and low-to-high fret sets.
steps: Play C major as frets 5–5–3 (notes C–E–G).
Move to F major as frets 5–6–5 (notes C–F–A).
Name the retained C and the two moving voices.
Find an alternative voicing and compare total movement by semitones.
exercises.self_check: Can you show one common tone and explain how the other two voices move?

steps: Play C major as frets 5–5–3 (notes C–E–G).
Move to F major as frets 5–6–5 (notes C–F–A).
Name the retained C and the two moving voices.
Find an alternative voicing and compare total movement by semitones.

modules.title: Write a triad-led progression
outcomes: Arrange one progression in connected voices
Describe why each inversion was chosen
modules.explanation: The same chord sequence can feel different when you change register, inversion and how inner voices move. Arrange C–Am–F–G using three-note voicings, choosing a deliberate line in the highest voice.

exercises.title: Top-voice melody
exercises.setup: Use C–Am–F–G in any comfortable register and three-note voicings.
steps: Spell each chord: C–E–G, A–C–E, F–A–C, G–B–D.
Choose one inversion for each and write the highest note of every chord.
Change inversions to make a smoother or more dramatic highest-note line.
Record your chosen voicings and reasoning in a Workbook page.
exercises.self_check: Can you connect the highest notes as a purposeful melodic line without changing the chord roots?

steps: Spell each chord: C–E–G, A–C–E, F–A–C, G–B–D.
Choose one inversion for each and write the highest note of every chord.
Change inversions to make a smoother or more dramatic highest-note line.
Record your chosen voicings and reasoning in a Workbook page.

relationships.why: A familiar major scale makes the meaning of scale degrees 1, 3 and 5 easier to recognize.
Knowing a few note locations makes it easier to verify shapes instead of memorizing diagrams.
Hearing the major and minor third supports aural comparison; it need not precede building a chord.
Inversions rearrange the same chord members without changing the triad identity.
A voicing describes which octave/arrangement of chord tones is played.
Recognizing common chord tones supports economical movement between voices.
Moving inversions across the guitar is a distinct trainable application.

entries.one_line: Feel the space between beats—and choose exactly where your notes land.
entries.overview: A steady beat gives music its pulse. Subdivision divides each beat into smaller, evenly spaced parts: two eighths, three eighth-note triplets, or four sixteenths per quarter-note beat. Learn to hear those spaces and play in them without rushing or dragging. The beat stays put while the pattern inside it changes.
entries.key_distinction: Tempo is the speed of the reference beat; meter organizes beats; subdivision divides a beat. Switching subdivision at the same quarter-note BPM is not automatically metric modulation or a meter change. Straight eighth-note triplets are not a universal definition of swing.

intro.text: is the pulse you can tap.
divides that pulse into smaller, evenly spaced parts.

learning_levels.title: Foundational
learning_levels.goal: Feel a steady quarter-note beat and count simple straight subdivisions without changing the pulse.

learning_levels.title: Intermediate
learning_levels.goal: Move between different subdivisions, keep an internal count through silence and place accents off the beat.

learning_levels.title: Advanced
learning_levels.goal: Reframe subdivision across uneven groupings, displaced accents and expressive rhythm-density changes.

applications.title: Listening & internal pulse
applications.summary: Hear the beat and its subdivision without depending on note pitches.

applications.title: Picking & coordination
applications.summary: Align pick attacks with even subdivision grids.

applications.title: Groove & accents
applications.summary: Separate an underlying beat from where attacks are emphasized.

applications.title: Counting & notation
applications.summary: Understand subdivision counts, rests and odd-meter grouping.

applications.title: Composing rhythm
applications.summary: Use changes in rhythmic density to develop a musical idea.

modules.title: Find the steady pulse
outcomes: Keep a steady pulse
Distinguish beat from subdivision
modules.explanation: The pulse is the even beat you can tap your foot to. Subdivision does not replace that pulse: it fits smaller, evenly spaced sounds inside each beat.

exercises.title: Find the steady pulse
exercises.setup: Use the 4/4 rhythm reference at 72 BPM with quarter notes, then eighths.
steps: Listen to four steady clicks and say “1, 2, 3, 4.”
Continue tapping once per click while quietly saying “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and.”
Stop speaking the “ands,” but keep your foot moving at the same rate.
Listen again: are the numbered beats still in the same places?
exercises.self_check: Can you keep the foot-tap steady when the subdivision doubles?

steps: Listen to four steady clicks and say “1, 2, 3, 4.”
Continue tapping once per click while quietly saying “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and.”
Stop speaking the “ands,” but keep your foot moving at the same rate.
Listen again: are the numbered beats still in the same places?

modules.title: Two notes per beat
outcomes: Count eight even events in 4/4
Coordinate alternate pick strokes to an eighth grid
modules.explanation: Straight eighth notes divide each quarter-note beat into two equal parts. At 80 BPM, the beat lasts 0.75 seconds; each eighth-note interval lasts 0.375 seconds.

exercises.title: Two notes per beat
exercises.setup: Use a comfortably muted guitar string in standard or any preferred tuning.
steps: Set the example to 80 BPM and choose eighth notes.
Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” aloud.
Pick one muted string on each count, alternating down and up strokes.
Switch back to quarter notes without changing the tempo.
exercises.self_check: Can you keep two even pick attacks inside each quarter-note beat?

steps: Set the example to 80 BPM and choose eighth notes.
Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” aloud.
Pick one muted string on each count, alternating down and up strokes.
Switch back to quarter notes without changing the tempo.

modules.title: Four spaces inside a beat
outcomes: Count a sixteenth-note grid
Maintain the quarter-note pulse
modules.explanation: Straight sixteenth notes divide one beat into four equal parts. Count each beat as “1 e and a”; all four sounds are evenly spaced, even when you choose not to play every space.

exercises.title: Four spaces inside a beat
exercises.setup: Use a slow pulse first; accuracy matters more than speed.
steps: Choose sixteenth notes with the quarter-note tempo at 64 BPM.
Speak each group: “1 e and a, 2 e and a...”
Tap once on each numbered beat while counting all sixteen positions.
Play only the numbered beats, but continue thinking the smaller divisions.
exercises.self_check: Do the numbered beats keep their places while you count 16 subdivisions?

steps: Choose sixteenth notes with the quarter-note tempo at 64 BPM.
Speak each group: “1 e and a, 2 e and a...”
Tap once on each numbered beat while counting all sixteen positions.
Play only the numbered beats, but continue thinking the smaller divisions.

modules.title: Read a one-bar count grid
outcomes: Identify beats in 4/4
Explain subdivision count without changing meter
modules.explanation: A 4/4 measure contains four quarter-note beats. It can be mapped into four, eight, twelve, or sixteen equal positions depending on the subdivision. Notation and the count grid are two ways to describe the same timing.

exercises.title: Read a one-bar count grid
exercises.setup: Use the on-screen 4/4 diagram without an instrument.
steps: Set the rhythm reference to quarter notes, and label all four beats.
Switch to eighth notes and count eight equally spaced positions.
Switch to triplets and count twelve positions in the same four-beat measure.
Explain why the number of beats stayed at four.
exercises.self_check: Can you distinguish beat count (four) from grid positions (four, eight, twelve, or sixteen)?

steps: Set the rhythm reference to quarter notes, and label all four beats.
Switch to eighth notes and count eight equally spaced positions.
Switch to triplets and count twelve positions in the same four-beat measure.
Explain why the number of beats stayed at four.

modules.title: Hear three inside one
outcomes: Hear two-vs-three subdivision
Distinguish straight triplet from swung eighth phrasing
modules.explanation: An eighth-note triplet divides each quarter-note beat into three equal parts, which is different from the two equal parts of straight eighth notes. A triplet is not automatically the same thing as swung eighth notes.

exercises.title: Hear three inside one
exercises.setup: Start with a quarter-note pulse of 72 BPM.
steps: Listen to eighth notes at 72 BPM, then choose eighth-note triplets.
Keep tapping four quarter-note beats while you speak “1 trip let, 2 trip let...”
Alternate the two and three-part patterns without changing the tap.
Record or replay the switch and listen for any unintended speeding up.
exercises.self_check: Can you switch from two equal notes per beat to three without shifting the beat?

steps: Listen to eighth notes at 72 BPM, then choose eighth-note triplets.
Keep tapping four quarter-note beats while you speak “1 trip let, 2 trip let...”
Alternate the two and three-part patterns without changing the tap.
Record or replay the switch and listen for any unintended speeding up.

modules.title: Move between eighths and sixteenths
outcomes: Preserve tempo when density changes
Control alternate-picking subdivisions
modules.explanation: Switching from two attacks per beat to four changes the number of attacks, not the tempo. The number you tap or count stays in the same place throughout the switch.

exercises.title: Move between eighths and sixteenths
exercises.setup: Mute a guitar string with the fretting hand so pitch is not a distraction.
steps: Choose 72 BPM, and pick straight eighths for one bar.
Switch to sixteenths for one bar while tapping the same four quarter beats.
Alternate one bar of each subdivision for four cycles.
Notice and correct any rushing during the transition.
exercises.self_check: Can you double the attack rate without speeding up the underlying beats?

steps: Choose 72 BPM, and pick straight eighths for one bar.
Switch to sixteenths for one bar while tapping the same four quarter beats.
Alternate one bar of each subdivision for four cycles.
Notice and correct any rushing during the transition.

modules.title: Accents move; the beat does not
outcomes: Distinguish accents from pulse
Practice a simple offbeat accent pattern
modules.explanation: An accent is emphasis on a note. Try placing accents on the “ands” of eighth notes, while continuing to feel the numbered quarter-note beats. This creates offbeat energy without necessarily changing tempo or meter.

exercises.title: Accents move; the beat does not
exercises.setup: Use one muted string or a quiet percussive strum.
steps: Count straight eighths at 80 BPM.
Play one muted note per eighth-note position.
Accent only the “ands”: 1-AND 2-AND 3-AND 4-AND.
Return to accented numbered beats and compare the feel.
exercises.self_check: Are your strong attacks on the offbeats while the numbered beats remain steady?

steps: Count straight eighths at 80 BPM.
Play one muted note per eighth-note position.
Accent only the “ands”: 1-AND 2-AND 3-AND 4-AND.
Return to accented numbered beats and compare the feel.

modules.title: Hear the notes you do not play
outcomes: Preserve a silent internal subdivision grid
Place sparse attacks correctly
modules.explanation: Rests and gaps are part of rhythmic timing. A sixteenth-note grid can continue underneath a phrase with only a few audible notes. Learning to count silent spaces keeps syncopated rhythms from drifting.

exercises.title: Hear the notes you do not play
exercises.setup: Use 60–70 BPM and a muted string; 4/4 meter.
steps: Count one bar of sixteenths slowly.
Play only on “1”, the “a” after 2, and “4 and.”
Say the unplayed count positions quietly or internally.
Repeat while keeping the same foot tap on 1, 2, 3, 4.
exercises.self_check: Can you place attacks accurately after silence without guessing?

steps: Count one bar of sixteenths slowly.
Play only on “1”, the “a” after 2, and “4 and.”
Say the unplayed count positions quietly or internally.
Repeat while keeping the same foot tap on 1, 2, 3, 4.

modules.title: Displace the accent by one sixteenth
outcomes: Move accents independently of the pulse
Maintain a stable reference beat
modules.explanation: A short rhythmic motif can sound transformed when its accents begin a sixteenth later. The motif shifts, but the reference quarter-note pulse and the 4/4 measure do not.

exercises.title: Displace the accent by one sixteenth
exercises.setup: Use muted picking, claps, or a single-pitch riff.
steps: Count one bar of straight sixteenths at 64 BPM.
Accent the first position of each beat for one bar.
Shift each accent forward one sixteenth (“e” positions) in the next bar.
Alternate the two bars without changing your foot tap.
exercises.self_check: Can you clearly hear accent displacement while retaining the same downbeats?

steps: Count one bar of straight sixteenths at 64 BPM.
Accent the first position of each beat for one bar.
Shift each accent forward one sixteenth (“e” positions) in the next bar.
Alternate the two bars without changing your foot tap.

modules.title: Change the grid without changing the pulse
outcomes: Move between three- and four-part subdivision
Keep reference tempo stable
modules.explanation: Moving between straight sixteenths and eighth-note triplets requires changing from four equal subdivisions per quarter to three, while holding the quarter note steady.

exercises.title: Change the grid without changing the pulse
exercises.setup: Use one muted string and focus on rhythmic accuracy rather than pitch.
steps: Tap four quarter notes at 72 BPM.
Pick four equal sixteenths per beat for one bar.
Switch to three equally spaced triplets per beat for the next bar.
Repeat the alternation and check whether the quarter-note tap shifts.
exercises.self_check: Can you alternate four-per-beat and three-per-beat attacks cleanly at one tempo?

steps: Tap four quarter notes at 72 BPM.
Pick four equal sixteenths per beat for one bar.
Switch to three equally spaced triplets per beat for the next bar.
Repeat the alternation and check whether the quarter-note tap shifts.

modules.title: Bring the skill into an odd meter
outcomes: Apply steady subdivision to 7/8
Hear grouping versus pulse
modules.explanation: Subdivision also applies in uneven meters. In a seven-eighths passage grouped 2+2+3, the eighth-note units can remain equal while the accents define an asymmetrical larger pattern. This example is conceptual; the interactive player demonstrates only 4/4.

exercises.title: Bring the skill into an odd meter
exercises.setup: Use a seven-eighths practice phrase; do not use the on-page 4/4 audio player as evidence for odd meter.
steps: Count seven equal eighth-note positions as 1-2 | 1-2 | 1-2-3.
Clap the start of each group, keeping the eighths even.
Play a short seven-eighths figure and repeat it without adding an eighth note.
Compare grouping changes such as 3+2+2 while preserving seven equal eighths.
exercises.self_check: Can you keep all seven eighth-note intervals equal while changing accent grouping?

steps: Count seven equal eighth-note positions as 1-2 | 1-2 | 1-2-3.
Clap the start of each group, keeping the eighths even.
Play a short seven-eighths figure and repeat it without adding an eighth note.
Compare grouping changes such as 3+2+2 while preserving seven equal eighths.

modules.title: Build tension with rhythmic density
outcomes: Use subdivision to shape a musical phrase
Separate density from BPM
modules.explanation: Composers can create energy by increasing the number of attacks without increasing tempo. A phrase may move from quarter notes to eighths to sixteenths while its quarter-note pulse stays steady.

exercises.title: Build tension with rhythmic density
exercises.setup: Use a Workbook, pencil, or muted guitar at 70–90 BPM.
steps: Write a three-bar idea in 4/4 using one harmony or pitch.
Use quarter notes in bar one, eighth notes in bar two, and sixteenths in bar three.
Keep the quarter-note pulse constant; add rests if the pattern feels crowded.
Play the phrase and describe where the energy changed.
exercises.self_check: Can you create more rhythmic activity while preserving the tempo throughout?

steps: Write a three-bar idea in 4/4 using one harmony or pitch.
Use quarter notes in bar one, eighth notes in bar two, and sixteenths in bar three.
Keep the quarter-note pulse constant; add rests if the pattern feels crowded.
Play the phrase and describe where the energy changed.

relationships.why: Understanding an even quarter-note pulse makes subdivision easier to hear.
Straight eighth-note counting offers a first two-part grid.
Three equal parts per beat introduce a different grid from straight eighths.
Swing is related to subdivision but must not be automatically equated with exact triplets.
Offbeat emphasis depends on knowing where the underlying pulse falls.
Backbeat accents are an accessible way to hear beat emphasis.
Accurate subdivision makes the timing of displaced attacks easier to control.
Subdivision can transfer to uneven meter patterns when grouping is explicitly taught.
Moving attacks by small rhythmic offsets requires a steady subdivision reference.
Changes of rhythmic unit can support metric modulation, but merely switching subdivision is not itself metric modulation.
